mcp_peer._note: 10 retries, 5 s apart — about 45 s of persistence, deliberately generous. Opponents run ngrok and other free tunnels that drop connections; we run a named tunnel and stay put, so the flakiness is nearly always theirs, and giving up after ~10 s forfeited four mini-games in a real match. The ceiling is THEIR watchdog, not our patience: the agreed watchdog_timeout_sec is 60, so past roughly 45 s of retrying they have already scored the turn against us and further attempts cannot win the game — they only delay our own scoring of it. Being generous up to that line is free; going beyond it is not. deadline_seconds 45 is what MAKES that true: the retry count alone never bounded anything, because each attempt carries its own 30 s call timeout and PeerSession reconnects once inside it, so ten attempts could occupy 645 s against a 60 s watchdog. The cap is on total wall clock, not on the interval - Table 19 binds the interval at a 5 s MINIMUM and we keep it, so this is stricter on us and never looser.

anthropic._note: max_retries 1: a hint is optional and has a zero-token template floor beneath it, but the 30 s turn deadline is not optional. At the shared default of 3 retries 5 s apart, two unreachable vendors cost 20 s on the first hint of a match — measured — which is most of the deadline. retry_after_seconds stays at the Appendix F minimum because it is never reached: the gatekeeper only sleeps between attempts.

inbound_peer._note: INBOUND messages from the opponent. This is a flood backstop, not a throttle on play: the real protection against a peer filling memory is the bounded inbox queue, which refuses politely and does not grow. The ceiling was 120/min on the assumption that turns are human-paced; they are not — a turn costs us milliseconds, so two fast peers exceed 2/sec trivially. In a six-game rehearsal against the reference we rejected its legitimate turn mid-game, then timed out waiting for the message we had thrown away ourselves. Set far above anything honest play can reach.
